phy_edx.9.0.summary: Every atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged **nucleus** made of **protons** (relative charge +1, relative mass 1) and **neutrons** (relative charge 0, relative mass 1), surrounded by **electrons** (relative charge -1, very small relative mass of about 1/1836) arranged in shells. Because an atom has **equal numbers of protons and electrons** it has **no overall charge**. Almost all the mass is in the nucleus, while the electrons on the outside are the particles that can move from atom to atom, which is the basis of electric current in metals and of static electricity.

core.p: Edexcel 10.1 asks you to **describe the structure of the atom**, limited to the **position, mass and charge** of protons, neutrons and electrons. That means for each particle you must know three things: where it is, how heavy it is compared with the others, and what charge it carries.
bullets: Position: protons and neutrons in the **nucleus**; electrons **orbit the nucleus** in shells (energy levels).
Relative mass: proton **1**, neutron **1**, electron about **1/1836** (very small, often written as 'negligible' or 0.0005).
Relative charge: proton **+1**, neutron **0**, electron **-1**.
The atom as a whole is **neutral** because number of protons = number of electrons.

callouts.p: This three-by-three table is worth easy marks every year. Practise writing it out from memory.

core.h: The nuclear model of the atom
core.p: An atom is made of a very small central **nucleus** with electrons moving around it. The nucleus contains the protons and neutrons, so it is **positively charged**. The electrons are arranged in **shells** (energy levels) at different distances from the nucleus.
bullets: Nucleus = protons + neutrons (together called **nucleons**).
The nucleus is **positive** because protons are positive and neutrons have no charge.
Electrons are **negative** and are found outside the nucleus.
The negative electrons are held in the atom by **electrostatic attraction** to the positive nucleus.

callouts.p: The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, containing protons and neutrons.

fig.cap: A lithium atom (lithium-7): the nucleus contains 3 protons and 4 neutrons, and 3 electrons are arranged in shells around it. The drawing is not to scale: the real nucleus is far smaller compared with the atom.

core.p: Charges are given as **relative charges**, comparing each particle with the proton. A proton and an electron carry charges of the **same size but opposite sign**, which is why equal numbers of them cancel out exactly.
bullets: Proton: **+1** (positive).
Electron: **-1** (negative).
Neutron: **0** (neutral, hence the name).
The actual size of the charge on a proton or electron is very small (1.6 x 10^-19 C), but at GCSE you mainly use relative values.

callouts.p: Protons and electrons have the same size of charge but very different masses. Do not mix these up.

core.p: Masses are also given as **relative masses**, compared with a proton. Protons and neutrons have almost exactly the same mass, so both are given relative mass 1. An electron is about **1836 times lighter** than a proton, so its mass is tiny in comparison.
bullets: Proton: relative mass **1**.
Neutron: relative mass **1**.
Electron: relative mass about **1/1836** (about 0.0005).
So **almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus**.

callouts.p: For the mass of an electron, mark schemes accept 'very small', 'negligible', '1/1836' or '0.0005'. Do not write 0 on its own.

core.p: In a neutral atom the number of electrons **equals** the number of protons. Each proton's +1 is cancelled by an electron's -1, so the total charge is zero. Neutrons do not affect the charge at all.
bullets: Total charge = (number of protons x +1) + (number of electrons x -1).
Equal numbers -> total charge 0.
The number of neutrons can be different from the number of protons without changing the charge.
Example: carbon has 6 protons, 6 electrons (and usually 6 neutrons) -> neutral.

callouts.p: Atoms have no overall charge because they contain equal numbers of positive protons and negative electrons.

core.h: Size of the atom and nucleus
core.p: Atoms are tiny, with a radius of about **1 x 10^-10 m**. The nucleus is much smaller still, tens of thousands of times smaller across than the atom. So an atom is **mostly empty space**, with nearly all its mass packed into the tiny nucleus.
bullets: Atom radius: about 1 x 10^-10 m (0.1 nm).
Nucleus: tens of thousands of times smaller across than the atom.
If the nucleus were the size of a pea, the atom would be about the size of a football stadium.
The nucleus is therefore **extremely dense**.

fig.cap: Sizes compared: the atom has a radius of about 1 x 10^-10 m, while the nucleus at the centre is tens of thousands of times smaller across, so most of the atom is empty space. Even this drawing exaggerates the size of the nucleus.

core.p: Two numbers describe the make-up of an atom's nucleus. The **atomic number** (proton number) is the number of protons, which decides which element it is. The **mass number** (nucleon number) is the total number of protons plus neutrons.
bullets: Atomic number Z = number of protons (= number of electrons in a neutral atom).
Mass number A = number of protons + number of neutrons.
Number of neutrons = A - Z.
Electrons are not counted in the mass number because their mass is negligible.

callouts.p: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

core.p: Electrons are on the outside of the atom and are less tightly held than the protons in the nucleus, so they can be **gained or lost**. An atom that has gained or lost electrons is an **ion** and has an overall charge.
bullets: **Lose** electrons -> more protons than electrons -> **positive ion**.
**Gain** electrons -> more electrons than protons -> **negative ion**.
The number of protons does **not** change when an ion forms, so it is still the same element.
Protons cannot be moved by rubbing or by a circuit because they are locked in the nucleus.

callouts.p: Objects become charged by transfer of electrons only. Answers that say protons move score zero.

fig.cap: A lithium atom has 3 protons and 3 electrons, so no overall charge. If it loses one electron it becomes a Li+ ion with 3 protons but only 2 electrons, giving an overall charge of +1.

core.p: This spec point opens the electricity topic because **electric current is a flow of charge**, and in metals the moving charges are **electrons**. Some electrons in metals are free to move between atoms (delocalised or free electrons), so metals are good electrical conductors.
bullets: In a metal wire, the charge carriers are **free electrons** (negative).
Electrons flow from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal of a cell.
Conventional current is shown from + to -, the opposite direction to electron flow.
In insulators, electrons are not free to move, so no current flows.
Static electricity is also caused by electrons being transferred between objects.

callouts.p: In metals, current is a flow of negatively charged electrons, because they are the only particles free to move.

core.p: Opposite charges attract and like charges repel. The negatively charged electrons are attracted towards the positively charged nucleus, which keeps them in the atom. Electrons in the outer shells are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are the easiest to remove.
bullets: Electron (-) and nucleus (+): **attract**.
Electron and electron: repel.
Outer electrons are held most weakly -> lost first.
This is why it is always electrons, not protons, that move in circuits and in charging.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare two particles. Always compare the same property directly, using comparative words.
bullets: Proton vs neutron: **same mass**, but proton is positive and neutron is neutral; both in the nucleus.
Proton vs electron: **equal and opposite charge**, but the electron is much lighter and is outside the nucleus.
Neutron vs electron: neutron is much heavier and uncharged; electron is negative and outside the nucleus.

head: Comparison
Similarity
Difference
rows: Same relative mass (1); both in nucleus
Opposite sign; electron about 1/1836 of the mass; different positions
Neutron mass 1 and neutral; electron negligible mass and -1

callouts.p: Use phrases like 'much smaller mass than' and 'opposite charge to' to earn comparison marks.

core.p: Questions on atomic structure are usually short recall items, but they can be combined with electricity questions. Be precise about which particle you mean.
bullets: Always name the particle: say 'electrons', not 'charges' or 'particles'.
Give relative values with signs: +1, 0, -1.
Say 'in the nucleus' or 'in shells around the nucleus' for position.
For neutral atoms, explain using equal numbers of protons and electrons.

callouts.p: Electrons are outside the nucleus. Writing that electrons are in the nucleus is a common lost mark.

analogy.t: A stadium with a marble in the middle
analogy.p: Picture a huge football stadium with a heavy marble on the centre spot. The marble is the nucleus: tiny but holding nearly all the mass and all the positive charge. Specks of dust flying around the stands are the electrons: almost weightless, negative, and far from the centre, with the rest of the stadium empty space. Where it breaks down: electrons do not fly around in neat paths like dust or planets; they are held by electrostatic attraction, not by walls, and the real nucleus is even smaller relative to the atom than a marble in a stadium.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element, made of a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it.
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and relative charge +1.
A particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and no charge.
A particle in shells around the nucleus with relative charge -1 and a very small relative mass (about 1/1836).
A proton or a neutron, the particles found in the nucleus.
A region at a set distance from the nucleus where electrons are found.
The mass of a particle compared with the mass of a proton.
The charge of a particle compared with the charge on a proton.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Having no overall charge because positive and negative charges are equal.
An atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons, so it has an overall charge.
An electron in a metal that is not bound to one atom and can move through the metal, carrying current.
The force of attraction between opposite charges, which holds electrons in an atom.

mistakes.w: Electrons are found in the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Electrons are in shells (energy levels) around/outside the nucleus; only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.

mistakes.w: The mass of an electron is 0.
mistakes.r: The electron has a very small (negligible) relative mass of about 1/1836, not zero.

mistakes.w: An atom is neutral because it has equal protons and neutrons.
mistakes.r: An atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

mistakes.w: A positive ion has gained protons.
mistakes.r: A positive ion has lost electrons; the number of protons does not change.
Protons and neutrons both have relative mass 1.
The nucleus is positive because it contains positive protons and neutral neutrons.

mistakes.w: Current in a wire is a flow of protons.
mistakes.r: Current in a metal is a flow of (free) electrons; protons stay in the nucleus.

exam.q: State the relative charge of a neutron.
model: 0 / zero / no charge.
exam.tip: Write 0, not 'neutral charge of 1'.

exam.q: Name the particle in an atom that has the smallest mass.
model: Electron.
exam.tip: Just the name is needed.

exam.q: State where protons are found in an atom.
model: In the nucleus.
exam.tip: One word answer: nucleus.

exam.q: Complete the table showing the relative mass and relative charge of a proton and an electron.
model: Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
Electron: relative mass 1/1836 (negligible), relative charge -1.
exam.tip: Signs on charges are needed for the mark.

exam.q: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
model: The number of protons equals the number of electrons.
Protons are positive and electrons are negative with the same size of charge, so they cancel.
exam.tip: Mention both equal numbers and opposite charges.

exam.q: Compare a proton with an electron. Refer to mass, charge and position.
model: Proton has much larger mass (relative mass 1) than electron (about 1/1836).
Proton charge +1, electron charge -1 (same size, opposite sign).
Proton is in the nucleus; electron is in shells around the nucleus.
exam.tip: One mark per property; compare directly.

exam.q: An atom of sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
model: 11 protons.
12 neutrons (23 - 11).
11 electrons.
exam.tip: Neutral atom: electrons = protons.

exam.q: Explain why almost all the mass of an atom is in its nucleus.
model: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, each of relative mass 1.
Electrons have a negligible / very small mass (about 1/1836).
exam.tip: Link location to mass.

exam.q: A neutral atom loses two electrons. State and explain the overall charge on the particle formed.
model: It now has two more protons than electrons (protons unchanged).
exam.tip: Charge sign plus reason.

exam.q: Describe the structure of an atom. Your answer should include the position, relative mass and relative charge of each particle, and explain why atoms are neutral and why electrons, not protons, are the particles that move in a metal wire.
model: Atom has a small central nucleus surrounded by electrons in shells.
Nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
Electron: very small relative mass (about 1/1836), relative charge -1.
Atom is neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
Protons are held in the nucleus and cannot move between atoms.
Some electrons in metals are free / outer electrons are held weakly, so electrons carry the current.
exam.tip: Cover all three particles fully, then the two explanations.

worked.q: An atom of aluminium has 13 protons and 14 neutrons. Find its atomic number, mass number and number of electrons, and state its overall charge.
worked.ans: Atomic number 13, mass number 27, 13 electrons, overall charge 0.

worked.q: A chlorine atom (17 protons, 18 neutrons) gains one electron. Calculate the relative charge of the particle and its relative mass to the nearest whole number.
steps: Electron mass is negligible, so relative mass is about 35.
worked.ans: Charge -1 (a negative ion); relative mass about 35.

worked.q: How many electrons have the same total mass as one proton? Use this to explain why electrons are left out of the mass number.
steps: Even a large atom has far fewer than 1836 electrons, so their total mass is a tiny fraction of the nucleus mass.
So mass number counts only protons and neutrons.
worked.ans: About 1836 electrons; their mass is negligible compared with the nucleus.

phy_edx.9.1.summary: Circuit diagrams use **standard symbols** so that anyone can read and build a circuit; you must be able to draw and recognise the symbols for cells, batteries, switches, voltmeters, ammeters, resistors, variable resistors, lamps, motors, diodes, thermistors, LDRs and LEDs. Components can be joined in **series** (one single loop, so the **same current** passes through every component and the supply p.d. is **shared**) or in **parallel** (separate branches, so each branch has the **same p.d.** as the supply and the current **splits**). A **voltmeter** measures potential difference in **volts (V)** and must always be connected **in parallel** across the component.

core.p: Edexcel 10.2 to 10.4 ask you to **draw and use circuit diagrams** with the correct symbols and the conventions for positive and negative terminals, to **describe the differences between series and parallel circuits**, and to **recall that a voltmeter is connected in parallel** with a component to measure the potential difference across it, in volts.
bullets: Draw symbols neatly with a ruler; wires are **straight lines** with no gaps.
Show the **positive terminal** of a cell as the **longer line**.
Know the series and parallel rules for current and potential difference.
Voltmeter: **in parallel**, measures p.d. in **volts (V)**.

callouts.p: Symbols, series vs parallel, voltmeter in parallel. Every Paper 2 electricity question builds on these.

core.p: A circuit diagram is a simplified map of a real circuit. Standard symbols mean the diagram can be understood by anyone in any country, and it shows clearly how the components are **connected**, which is what really matters, not what they look like.
bullets: Wires are drawn as straight lines, usually forming rectangles.
A **dot** at a junction shows that wires are joined.
There must be a **complete circuit** (closed loop) for a current to flow.
The layout on paper does not need to match the real positions of components.

callouts.p: In 'complete the circuit' questions, make sure every line meets the next with no gaps, or the circuit is not complete.

core.p: The energy source in most circuits is a **cell** or a **battery**. A battery is **two or more cells** joined together. The **long thin line** is the positive (+) terminal and the **short thick line** is the negative (-) terminal. A **switch** opens or closes a gap in the circuit.
bullets: **Cell**: one long line and one short line.
**Battery**: two or more cells joined in series (sometimes drawn with a dashed line between).
**Open switch**: gap in the circuit, so no current flows.
**Closed switch**: complete path, so current can flow.
Conventional current flows out of the **positive** terminal, round the circuit, and back to the negative terminal.

callouts.p: The longer line of a cell is positive. Students often get this backwards when drawing diodes the right way round.

core.p: Lamps, motors and resistors are the components that transfer energy or control the current. Learn each symbol exactly, because similar-looking symbols mean very different things.
bullets: **Lamp**: circle with a cross inside; transfers energy by light (and heating).
**Resistor**: rectangle; a fixed resistance that limits the current.
**Variable resistor**: rectangle with a diagonal arrow through it; resistance can be changed to vary the current.
**Motor**: circle with an M; transfers energy to a kinetic store.

head: Component
Symbol description
Job
rows: Gives out light, one way only

core.p: Meters are drawn as circles with a letter: **A** for an ammeter and **V** for a voltmeter. Diodes, LEDs, LDRs and thermistors are made from semiconductors. Their symbols are all based on either the diode triangle or the resistor rectangle.
bullets: **Diode**: triangle pointing in the direction current can flow, against a bar; current flows only one way.
**LED** (light-emitting diode): diode symbol with two arrows pointing **away**, because it gives out light.
**LDR** (light-dependent resistor): resistor inside a circle with two arrows pointing **in**, because light falls on it.
**Thermistor**: resistor with a diagonal line with a short flat tail, its resistance depends on temperature.

callouts.p: Arrows pointing out = light goes out (LED). Arrows pointing in = light comes in (LDR).

core.p: In a **series circuit** all the components are connected **one after another in a single loop**. There is only one path, so the charge has to pass through every component in turn.
bullets: **Current is the same** at every point in a series circuit.
The **p.d. of the supply is shared** between the components: V_total = V1 + V2 + ...
The **total resistance is the sum** of the individual resistances: R_total = R1 + R2.
If one component breaks or is removed, the circuit is broken and **everything stops**.
Adding more lamps in series makes each lamp **dimmer**, because the total resistance increases and the current decreases.

callouts.p: Components connected end to end in a single loop, so there is only one path for the current.

core.p: In a **parallel circuit** the components are on **separate branches**, each connected directly across the supply. Charge can take different paths, splitting at a **junction** and rejoining later.
bullets: The **p.d. across each branch is the same** as the supply p.d.
The **current splits** at junctions: total current = sum of the branch currents (I = I1 + I2).
Each branch can be **switched on and off independently**.
If one lamp breaks, the others **stay on**.
Adding another branch **reduces the total resistance**, so the total current from the supply **increases**.

callouts.p: Components connected on separate branches, each across the same two points, so there is more than one path for the current.

fig.cap: A parallel circuit: the two lamps are on separate branches. The current splits at the junction, and each lamp has the full supply p.d. across it, so each lamp is as bright as it would be on its own and can work independently.

core.p: The 'describe the differences' part of the spec is a favourite comparison question. Compare **current**, **potential difference**, **resistance** and **what happens if a component fails**.
bullets: Series: one path; parallel: more than one path.
Series: same current everywhere; parallel: current splits between branches.
Series: p.d. shared; parallel: same p.d. across each branch.
Series: adding resistors increases total resistance; parallel: adding resistors decreases total resistance.
Series: one fault stops everything; parallel: other branches keep working.

head: Feature
Series
Parallel
rows: Splits; branch currents add to total
Sum of resistances; increases when more added
Less than smallest branch resistance; decreases when more added
Each branch can have its own switch

callouts.p: Household lights and sockets are wired in parallel, so each gets the full mains p.d. and can be switched on and off independently.

core.p: A **voltmeter** measures the **potential difference (p.d.)**, also called voltage, across a component, in **volts (V)**. P.d. is a difference between two points, so the voltmeter must be connected **across** the component, **in parallel** with it, with one lead on each side.
bullets: Connect one terminal to each end of the component.
Do **not** break the circuit to add a voltmeter; add it on afterwards across the component.
A voltmeter has a **very high resistance**, so almost no current flows through it and it does not change the circuit.
If wrongly connected in series, its very high resistance would stop almost all the current.
The reading is in **volts (V)**.

callouts.p: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference, in volts, across it.

core.p: Although ammeters are covered in more detail in 10.7, exam questions often mix them up with voltmeters. An **ammeter** measures **current** in **amperes (A)** and is connected **in series**, so all the current passes through it.
bullets: Ammeter: in **series**, very **low resistance**, measures current in A.
Voltmeter: in **parallel**, very **high resistance**, measures p.d. in V.
Memory aid: 'Ammeters in A line, Voltmeters on the Verge (beside)'.

callouts.p: Saying a voltmeter is in series, or an ammeter in parallel, loses the mark every time.

core.h: Drawing circuit diagrams in the exam
core.p: Many questions ask you to draw a circuit to carry out an investigation, for example to find how the current through a lamp changes with p.d. Use a clear, standard layout.
bullets: Draw the supply (cell or battery), then a **single loop** containing the component, an ammeter and a variable resistor (to change the current).
Add the **voltmeter in parallel** across the component last.
Use a ruler and draw symbols the right size; label if unsure.
Check: complete loop, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel, correct symbols.

callouts.p: Typically 1 mark for correct symbols, 1 for ammeter in series, 1 for voltmeter in parallel across the component, 1 for a way to vary the p.d. (variable resistor or variable supply).

core.p: Grade 9 answers explain **why** the rules are true using charge and energy. In series there is only one path, so the same charge must pass through each component (same current), and the energy each coulomb gets from the supply is shared between the components (p.d. shared). In parallel each coulomb goes through only one branch, so it transfers all its energy in that branch (same p.d. across each branch).
bullets: Same current in series: charge is not used up, and there is nowhere else for it to go.
Current splits in parallel: charge is conserved at junctions, so branch currents add up to the total.
P.d. shared in series: energy per coulomb supplied is divided between the components.
Same p.d. in parallel: each branch is connected directly across the supply.

analogy.p: A series circuit is like a single-lane road through several towns: every car (charge) must pass through every town, so the traffic flow (current) is the same everywhere, and if one bridge closes, the whole route stops. A parallel circuit is like a motorway that splits into several separate roads: cars choose one road, the traffic divides at the junction and rejoins later, and a closed road does not stop traffic on the others. A voltmeter is like a surveyor comparing the height of the road before and after a hill: they stand beside the road and do not block it. Where it breaks down: cars use up fuel and can park, but charge is never used up and current in a series circuit is the same everywhere instantly; also the height-difference idea of p.d. is only a model of energy per unit charge.

terms.d: A drawing of a circuit using standard symbols to show how components are connected.
A single source of potential difference; the long line of its symbol is the positive terminal.
Two or more cells connected together.
A component that opens or closes a gap in a circuit to stop or allow a current.
A component that limits (reduces) the current in a circuit.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed, used to vary the current.
A component that allows current to flow in one direction only.
Light-emitting diode: a diode that gives out light when a current flows through it in the forward direction.
Light-dependent resistor: a resistor whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
A resistor whose resistance changes with temperature (for the common type, resistance decreases as temperature increases).
A circuit with all components in a single loop, so there is only one path for the current.
A circuit in which components are on separate branches connected across the same two points.
A point in a circuit where the current splits or joins.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V).
A meter connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference across it, in volts.
A meter connected in series to measure the current, in amperes.

mistakes.w: A voltmeter is connected in series with the component.
mistakes.r: A voltmeter is connected in parallel (across) the component.

mistakes.w: Voltmeter measures the current through the lamp.
mistakes.r: A voltmeter measures the potential difference across the component, in volts.

mistakes.w: Current is used up as it goes round a series circuit, so it is smaller after each lamp.
mistakes.r: Current is the same at all points in a series circuit; charge is not used up.

mistakes.w: In a parallel circuit the p.d. is shared between the branches.
mistakes.r: Each branch has the same p.d. as the supply; it is the current that splits.

mistakes.w: Drawing the LDR with arrows pointing out (or LED with arrows in).
mistakes.r: LDR arrows point in (light received); LED arrows point out (light emitted).

mistakes.w: Adding more resistors in parallel increases the total resistance.
mistakes.r: Adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance, because there are more paths for the charge.

mistakes.w: The short thick line of a cell is positive.
mistakes.r: The long thin line is the positive terminal; the short thick line is negative.

mistakes.w: A battery is the same as a cell.
mistakes.r: A battery is two or more cells joined together.

mistakes.w: Drawing a variable resistor as a resistor with an arrow touching it from the side.
mistakes.r: A variable resistor has a diagonal arrow drawn through the rectangle.

exam.q: Draw the circuit symbol for a light-dependent resistor (LDR).
model: Rectangle (resistor) inside a circle with two arrows pointing towards it.
exam.tip: Arrows must point in.

exam.q: State the unit of potential difference.
model: Volt (V).
exam.tip: Do not write 'voltage' as the unit.

exam.q: State how a voltmeter should be connected to measure the potential difference across a lamp.
model: In parallel with / across the lamp.
exam.tip: 'Across' and 'in parallel' are both accepted.

exam.q: Name the component whose symbol is a circle with a cross inside it.
model: (Filament) lamp.
exam.tip: Not 'bulb' if the question asks for the component name; 'lamp' is safest.

exam.q: Describe two differences between a series circuit and a parallel circuit.
model: Series has one path; parallel has more than one path / branches.
Current same everywhere in series but splits in parallel / p.d. shared in series but same across each branch in parallel / one fault stops all in series but not in parallel.
exam.tip: Each difference must mention both types of circuit.

exam.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series to a 6 V battery. State the p.d. across each lamp and explain your answer.
model: The supply p.d. is shared between components in series, and identical lamps share it equally.
exam.tip: Equal sharing only works for identical components.

exam.q: The same two lamps are now connected in parallel to the 6 V battery. State the p.d. across each lamp.
model: 6 V (each).
exam.tip: Parallel branches each get the full supply p.d.

exam.q: Explain why the lights in a house are connected in parallel rather than in series.
model: Each light gets the full (mains) p.d.
Each light can be switched on and off independently.
If one light fails, the others keep working.
exam.tip: Three separate advantages for three marks.

exam.q: Draw a circuit that could be used to measure the current through and the potential difference across a fixed resistor, with a way of changing the current.
model: Correct symbols for cell/battery and resistor in a complete loop.
Ammeter in series with the resistor.
Voltmeter in parallel across the resistor.
Variable resistor in series (or variable power supply).
exam.tip: Check each meter's position before you finish.

exam.q: A student builds a circuit with a battery, a switch, and three identical lamps. Lamp X is in the main circuit and lamps Y and Z are in parallel with each other. Explain what happens to the brightness of the lamps when lamp Z is removed. Use ideas about current, potential difference and resistance, and comment on how the circuit shows the differences between series and parallel connections.
model: Y and Z are in parallel, so removing Z leaves only one path for that part of the circuit.
The resistance of the parallel section increases (one branch instead of two).
So the total resistance of the circuit increases.
So the current from the battery (through X) decreases, and X gets dimmer.
The p.d. across X decreases, so the p.d. across Y increases (supply p.d. shared in series).
So Y gets brighter; X is in series, so all current passes through it, whereas Y and Z shared the current.
exam.tip: Work step by step: resistance first, then current, then the p.d. shares, then brightness.

worked.q: A 9 V battery is connected to a lamp and a resistor in series. A voltmeter across the resistor reads 5.5 V. What would a voltmeter across the lamp read?
steps: In series the supply p.d. is shared: V_supply = V_lamp + V_resistor.

worked.q: A 12 V supply is connected to three lamps in parallel. The branch currents are 0.5 A, 0.5 A and 1.0 A. Find the p.d. across each lamp and the current from the supply.
steps: In parallel, each branch has the same p.d. as the supply, so each lamp has 12 V across it.
Current splits at the junctions, so total current = sum of branch currents.
worked.ans: 12 V across each lamp; 2.0 A from the supply.

worked.q: Model answer: a student connects a voltmeter in series with a lamp and a cell. The lamp does not light and the voltmeter reads almost the full cell p.d. Explain why.
steps: A voltmeter has a very high resistance.
In series, all the current must pass through the voltmeter, so the current becomes almost zero.
With almost no current the lamp cannot light.
Almost all of the supply p.d. is across the very high resistance of the voltmeter, so it reads close to the cell p.d.
The voltmeter should be connected in parallel across the lamp instead.
worked.ans: The voltmeter's very high resistance in series stops the current; it must be connected in parallel.
